---
title: "Reading CSV files"
---

`read_csv()` reads a delimited text file into typed columns. It is the
native reader behind phibble's `DataFrame::fromCsv()`. Its records, names, guessed
types, values, and problem messages match phibble's PHP reader, which follows
readr 2 (`readr::read_delim()`). phibble keeps name repair, `col_select`, factor
and `parse_number()` columns, and the problems warning in PHP.

`Phit\read_csv()` is the narrower of the two readers. It has no `select` or
`name_repair` option, its `col_names` takes a boolean rather than a list of
names, and the readr letters `f` (factor) and `n` (number) have no type code
here. `DataFrame::fromCsv()` supplies all of these in PHP around the native
call.

```php
Phit\read_csv(string $path, array $options = []): array;
```

## Options

Every option is optional. The defaults are readr's.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `delimiter` | `','` | One byte. |
| `quote` | `'"'` | One byte, or `''` for no quoting. |
| `escape_double` | `true` | `""` inside quotes is one `"`. |
| `escape_backslash` | `false` | `\x` is `x`, inside and outside quotes. |
| `na` | `['', 'NA']` | Strings read as NA, compared after trimming. A quoted `"NA"` is also NA. |
| `trim_ws` | `true` | Trim spaces and tabs from values (and PHP `trim()` from header names). |
| `skip` | `0` | Raw lines skipped before the header. |
| `n_max` | `null` | Maximum number of data rows. |
| `comment` | `''` | Text from this prefix to the end of the line is ignored. A line that starts with it is dropped. |
| `skip_empty_rows` | `true` | Blank lines are skipped. When false, each is read as an ordinary record. |
| `col_names` | `true` | When false, the first record is data and the names are `X1`..`Xn`. |
| `types` | `[]` | Type codes keyed by 0-based column position. Missing positions are guessed. |
| `guess_max` | `1000` | Rows sampled for guessing. |
| `decimal_mark` | `'.'` | One byte. |
| `grouping_mark` | `null` | `null` uses `.` when the decimal mark is `,` and `,` otherwise. `''` means none. |
| `block_size` | `4194304` | Bytes read from the file at a time. The result does not depend on it; tests use small values. |

The type codes are `?` (guess), `l` (bool), `i` (int), `d` (double), `c`
(string), `D` (date), `T` (datetime), and `_` (skip). phibble reads `f`
(factor) and `n` (number) columns by requesting `c` and parsing in PHP.

## Result

```php
[
    'names' => list<string>,
    'columns' => list<null|array{
        type: 'bool'|'int'|'float'|'string'|'date'|'datetime',
        values: list<bool|int|float|string|null>,
        failed: int,
    }>,
    'problems' => list<string>,
]
```

Values use phibble's storage form. Bools, ints, and floats are PHP scalars and
strings are strings. A date is an int count of days since 1970-01-01. A
datetime is an int count of microseconds since the epoch in UTC. NA is `null`.
A skipped column is `null`. `failed` counts values that did not parse under the
column's explicit or guessed type; those values are `null`. phibble turns
nonzero counts into its `column 'x': n values could not be parsed as type`
problems.

`problems` holds one entry per ragged row, such as
`row 7: expected 5 columns, got 4`. The row number is the record's position in
the file, counting skipped lines and the header. A multi-line quoted field
counts as one record. A file that ends inside a quoted field adds
`row N: unterminated quoted field at end of file`.

## Reading in chunks

`Phit\CsvReader` reads a file a chunk of rows at a time. It is the native
reader behind phibble's `DataFrame::csvChunks()` and `fromCsvChunked()`, which
follow readr's `read_delim_chunked()`. It holds the text of one chunk and one
read block, so its memory follows the chunk size and not the file size.

```php
$reader = new Phit\CsvReader(string $path, array $options = []);
$reader->names(): array;           // list<string>
$reader->next(int $rows): ?array;  // the next chunk, or null
```

The options are `read_csv()`'s. The constructor reads the header, so
`names()` is available before the first chunk. It returns the header's names,
`X1`..`Xn` when `col_names` is false, or `[]` for an empty file. `next()`
returns at most `$rows` rows in `read_csv()`'s result shape, with two more
keys: `position`, the 1-based index of the chunk's first row, and `rows`, the
chunk's row count. It returns `null` once no rows remain.

Chunks follow phibble's chunked reader:

- Types not given in `types` are guessed from the first chunk, from
  `guess_max` of its rows sampled as above. Every later chunk is parsed as
  those types. phibble sets `guess_max` to the chunk size by default, as readr
  does. A value in a later chunk that does not fit its column's type counts in
  that chunk's `failed`.
- Problem rows are numbered from the start of the file. Each chunk carries the
  problems of its own rows.
- The unterminated-quote problem goes with the last chunk. After each chunk
  the reader looks past blank lines to see whether records remain.
- `n_max` caps the rows across all chunks.
- A file with no data rows gives no chunks. The one exception is an
  unterminated quote in the header: `next()` then returns a chunk with no rows
  that carries the problem.

## Records

- Short rows are padded with NA. Long rows put the extra fields, joined by the
  delimiter, into the last column.
- A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of the file is removed before
  tokenizing (when `skip` is 0), so a quoted first header loses its quotes.
  One at the start of the first record after skipped lines is also removed.
- LF and CRLF line endings are accepted. CR is read as the line ending when
  the first line break falls in a 4 MiB stretch of the file (counted from the
  first byte after skipped lines) that holds no LF. phibble reads 4 MiB blocks
  and decides from the first block with a line break, so the two agree.
  Otherwise a lone CR is data. Quoted fields can hold delimiters and
  line breaks, which are kept as written.
- A line is blank when its raw text holds nothing but spaces, tabs and
  carriage returns. That is the raw line and not the parsed fields, so a quoted
  empty string is a field holding data, and it does not depend on `trim_ws` or
  on the delimiter: a line of spaces is blank even when the delimiter is a
  space. Under `skip_empty_rows` a blank line is dropped; otherwise it is
  tokenized like any other line, so an empty line is one empty field and a
  wider data frame records it as one column short. A last line the file left
  unterminated is never dropped, so `a\n ` is two rows and `a\n \n` is one.
- An unterminated quote at the end of the file closes the field there.
- Bytes are passed through unchanged. There is no encoding validation.
- An empty file, or one with only empty lines, returns no names and no columns.
  When the header is read and no data rows are, the names come back with empty
  columns typed string, following readr, which reads a header-only file as
  text. Four cases reach that state: `n_max: 0`, a header-only file, a `skip`
  that leaves no row after the header, and every row empty under
  `skip_empty_rows`. An explicit code in `types` still applies.

phibble tokenizes by vroom's (readr 2's) quote rules with a fast reader when
it can (no comment, `""` escapes, no backslash escapes, and a quote character)
and with its own character-level reader otherwise. The native reader
reproduces both. The two differ in small ways:

- In the fast reader, a field is quoted when its first byte is the quote.
  Inside it, every lone quote toggles quoting and is dropped, and a doubled
  quote is a literal quote, so `"x "y" z"` reads as `x y z`. Quotes in an
  unquoted field are literal.
- The character-level reader folds CRLF to LF everywhere, including inside
  quotes. A quote opens a quoted section only when the field so far is
  whitespace. Text after the comment prefix ends the record, so a line holding
  only spaces and a comment is a one-field record holding those spaces, unless
  no record has been read yet: before the first one, a comment prefix with only
  whitespace in front of it drops the line, as readr drops it.

## Guessing

Values are trimmed and NA-mapped first. The guess uses every row when there are
at most `guess_max`. Otherwise it uses `guess_max - 1` evenly spaced rows
(`step = intdiv(rows, guess_max)`: rows 0, step, 2·step, and so on) plus the
last row, as vroom does. The first rule that fits every sampled value wins.

1. **bool**: `T F TRUE FALSE True False true false t f`.
2. **int**: an optional sign, then digits with optional grouping marks between
   them, that fits in 64 bits. An unsigned leading zero (`007`) stays text;
   `0` and `-07` are ints.
3. **double**: `[+-]inf` or `[+-]nan` (any case), or a decimal number with an
   optional decimal mark, exponent, and grouping marks. `1.` and `1,` qualify.
   The leading-zero rule applies: `0e5` and `00.5` stay text.
4. **date**: `YYYY-MM-DD` or `YYYY/MM/DD` (the separators may differ).
5. **datetime**: `YYYY-MM-DD[(T| )HH[:MM[:SS[.fraction]]]][Z|±HH[[:]MM]]`.
6. Otherwise **string**.

An all-NA column with at least one data row is bool. phibble differs from readr
in one rule: whole numbers guess as int, where readr guesses double. The date
and datetime rules check only the shape. A column whose values look like dates
guesses date even when a value is not a calendar date, and that value then
fails to parse.

## Parsing

The column's type is applied to every row. A guessed numeric column allows the
grouping mark. An explicitly typed one does not, as in phibble.

- **bool** also accepts `1` and `0`.
- **int** accepts leading zeros and a `+` sign.
- **double** accepts PHP numeric strings (when the decimal mark is `.`),
  `inf` and `nan`, and the guessing grammar.
- **date** needs a valid calendar date in years 0001 to 9999.
- **datetime** needs a valid date, hours up to 23, and minutes and seconds up
  to 59. Fractions are truncated to microseconds. An offset converts to UTC
  and no offset means UTC. Offsets up to ±24:59 are accepted, as by PHP's
  `DateTimeImmutable`. A date alone is midnight UTC.

## Errors

A missing or unreadable file and invalid options throw `\ValueError` (not the
statistical exception). Invalid options include an unknown key, a wrong value
type, a multi-byte delimiter, quote, decimal mark, or grouping mark, an unknown
type code, and a negative `skip` or `n_max`. The decimal and grouping marks
must differ and cannot be a digit, sign, `e`, `E`, or newline.

## Differences from readr

These follow phibble's reader:

- Whole numbers guess as int.
- With a comment prefix, a value followed by a comment is trimmed (`2 # x`
  reads as `2`).
- Date and datetime guessing checks the shape only.
- In a file whose only line ending is CR, readr skips a blank line only before
  the first record and keeps the interior and trailing ones; both readers read
  CR as the line ending and then apply the blank-line rule throughout.

## Performance

On an Apple Silicon Mac with PHP 8.5, a 1,000,000-row file with int, float,
string, date, and datetime columns (59 MB) reads in about 0.11 seconds,
including building the PHP arrays. phibble's `csv_guess` benchmark (1,000,000
rows) takes 0.12 seconds through `DataFrame::fromCsv()` with the extension and
1.0 seconds with phibble's PHP reader.

## Verification

`tests/csv.php` checks quoting, escapes, NA handling, trimming, every option,
every type code, the guessing rules, datetimes, ragged rows, chunks, and the
error cases.

`tests/csv-conformance.php` checks `read_csv()` against phibble's reader
without a phibble checkout. phibble generates `tests/fixtures/csv-conformance.json`
from its own PHP reader with `bin/generate-csv-conformance`, and this repository
commits a byte-identical copy. The file holds 108 cases: every option at its
default and at one other value, all eight type codes, ragged rows, a BOM, CRLF
and CR line endings, an unterminated quote, comments, an empty file, bytes that
are not valid UTF-8, the four ways to read no data rows, and the blank-line
rule in its eighteen shapes. Each case records
the input, the options, and the names, types, values, failure counts, and
problems phibble produces. The suite requires `read_csv()` to reproduce all of
it, so a change in either reader fails in its own repository. It reads every
case again at block sizes of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and 64 bytes, and through
`CsvReader` in one chunk and in chunks of 1, 2, and 3 rows. One chunk must
equal the whole read. Small chunks must give the same problems in order and,
read as text, the same values.

The copy is pinned. `tests/fixtures/PHIBBLE_REFERENCE` names the phibble commit
it came from, and `bin/fetch-csv-fixtures` copies the file from that commit,
either from a local checkout given as its first argument or in `PHIBBLE_REPO`,
or from a clone of the repository named in the pin. Refreshing the corpus means
regenerating it in phibble, moving the pin, and running that script.

phibble's reader does not report an unterminated quoted field and `read_csv()`
does. Each case therefore carries a closed list of the extra problems
`read_csv()` is expected to add, and the suite compares its problems with the
union rather than filtering by pattern, so an unexpected problem fails.

`tests/csv-phibble.php` is the deep tier and runs when `PHIBBLE_AUTOLOAD` points
at phibble's `vendor/autoload.php`. It compares both readers through
`DataFrame::fromCsv()` on the fixtures and on thousands of random files and
option combinations, with the case count and the seed taken from
`CSV_FUZZ_CASES` and `CSV_FUZZ_SEED`. It requires identical names, types,
values, and warnings. With a phibble that has `DataFrame::csvChunks()`, it also
compares `CsvReader` with phibble's PHP chunked reader on random files, chunk
sizes, and native block sizes (`CSV_CHUNK_CASES` of them). It requires the same
chunks, positions, types, values, and per-chunk warnings, in the same order.
